---
title: "Large panels and compressed regressions"
description: "Test whether small regression summaries preserve a large longitudinal experiment."
jupyter: python3
---

These simulations follow [Large Scale Longitudinal
Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09952) by Apoorva Lal, Alexander
Fischer, and Matthew Wardrop, with [public
code](https://github.com/py-econometrics/panel-at-scale-code). The simulations
test regression compression under several panel structures; storage and
distributed estimation are outside this example.

## Scientific question

Suppose raw longitudinal data are too large to centralize. A site can transmit
small regression summaries instead. A simulation should test whether those
summaries preserve the treatment-effect information under trends, serial
dependence, and heterogeneous effects.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from pypanelsim import designs
```

## Main panel design

The untreated outcome contains unit effects, time effects, unit-specific linear
trends, and AR(1) error. One cohort adopts treatment. The effect path can be
concave or another configured profile, with optional unit heterogeneity.

```{python}
config = designs.RegressionCompressionConfig(
    n_units=800,
    n_periods=35,
    adoption_period=15,
    n_treated=320,
    effect_profile="concave",
    max_effect=1.0,
    heterogeneous_effects=True,
)

panel = designs.regression_compression(config=config, seed=42)
print(panel.shape)
print(round(panel.true_att, 3))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-large-panel-design
#| fig-cap: "Observed outcomes and known event-time effects in the regression-compression design."
#| fig-alt: "A heatmap shows the large panel's observed outcomes, and a line chart shows the true event-time effect path."

order = np.argsort(panel.adoption_times, kind="stable")
event_truth = panel.truth.event_study(event_times=range(-10, 20))

figure, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5), constrained_layout=True)
outcome_image = axes[0].matshow(
    panel.outcome[order],
    aspect="auto",
    cmap="coolwarm",
)
axes[0].set_xlabel("period")
axes[0].set_ylabel("units, sorted by adoption")
axes[0].set_title("Observed outcome")
figure.colorbar(outcome_image, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.035, pad=0.02)

axes[1].plot(
    event_truth["event_time"],
    event_truth["effect"],
    marker="o",
)
axes[1].axhline(0.0, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
axes[1].axvline(-0.5, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.8)
axes[1].set_xlabel("event time")
axes[1].set_ylabel("true effect")
axes[1].set_title("Known event-study effects")
plt.show()
```

## A minimal compressed summary

For a regression $y=X\beta+u$, a site can summarize its data with
$X'X$, $X'y$, $y'y$, and the observation count. Sites can add these terms
without sharing rows.

The example below uses treatment, a post indicator, and their interaction. It
is deliberately small; an applied design would add its required fixed-effect
or basis representation.

```{python}
columns = panel.as_long_dict()
y = columns["outcome"]

post = (columns["time"] >= config.adoption_period).astype(float)
treated_unit = np.repeat(panel.ever_treated.astype(float), panel.n_periods)
x = np.column_stack(
    (
        np.ones(y.size),
        treated_unit,
        post,
        treated_unit * post,
    )
)

summary = {
    "n": y.size,
    "xtx": x.T @ x,
    "xty": x.T @ y,
    "yty": float(y @ y),
}

beta_from_summary = np.linalg.solve(summary["xtx"], summary["xty"])
beta_from_rows = np.linalg.lstsq(x, y, rcond=None)[0]

print(np.allclose(beta_from_summary, beta_from_rows))
print(np.round(beta_from_summary, 3))
```

This equality is algebraic for the stated regression. It does not show that
the interaction coefficient equals the desired dynamic-effect estimand.
Compression and causal identification are separate questions.

## Combine summaries across sites

```{python}
site_ids = np.array_split(np.arange(panel.n_units), 4)
site_summaries = []

for site_units in site_ids:
    rows = np.isin(columns["unit"], site_units)
    x_site = x[rows]
    y_site = y[rows]
    site_summaries.append((x_site.T @ x_site, x_site.T @ y_site))

pooled_xtx = sum(item[0] for item in site_summaries)
pooled_xty = sum(item[1] for item in site_summaries)
pooled_beta = np.linalg.solve(pooled_xtx, pooled_xty)

print(np.allclose(pooled_beta, beta_from_rows))
```

The partition has no effect because the summaries are additive.

## Anscombe-style stress tests

The Anscombe family changes panel structure while preserving selected low-order
summaries. It asks whether an analysis that sees only those summaries misses a
scientifically important difference.

```{python}
print(designs.available_anscombe_designs())

anscombe_config = designs.AnscombePanelConfig(
    n_units=400,
    n_periods=20,
)

for name in designs.available_anscombe_designs():
    draw = designs.anscombe(name, config=anscombe_config, seed=17)
    print(name, draw.shape, round(draw.true_att, 3))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-anscombe-effects
#| fig-cap: "Treatment effects for the four Anscombe-style panel variants."
#| fig-alt: "Four heatmaps compare treatment effects that share summary features but have different structures."

figure, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 8), constrained_layout=True)
for axis, name in zip(
    axes.ravel(),
    designs.available_anscombe_designs(),
    strict=True,
):
    draw = designs.anscombe(name, config=anscombe_config, seed=17)
    image = axis.matshow(draw.effect_surface, aspect="auto", cmap="coolwarm")
    axis.set_title(name.replace("_", " "))
    axis.set_xlabel("period")
    axis.set_ylabel("unit")
    figure.colorbar(image, ax=axis, fraction=0.04, pad=0.02)
plt.show()
```

The four variants are `zero`, `unit`, `time`, and `cohort_time`. They locate
heterogeneity at different levels.

## What to report

A compression experiment should report both layers:

- the causal design: assignment, untreated outcomes, potential effects, and target;
- the transmitted summary: regressors, sufficient statistics, grouping, and
  numeric precision.

A small communication cost is not useful if the summary corresponds to the
wrong regression or the regression corresponds to the wrong causal target.
